nodes.label: Heat Stress Effects on Poultry (Four-Quadrant Diagram)
nodes.description: Conceptual diagram: a sun radiating three curved yellow arrows onto a chicken at the centre, surrounded by four labelled quadrants that enumerate the consequences of heat stress - Behavioral Changes (top-left), Neuroendocrine changes (top-right), Physiological Changes (bottom-left) and Production changes (bottom-right). The sun-to-bird arrows encode the causal direction: thermal load drives all four response categories.
nodes.rationale: The radial layout is chosen to show that a single environmental stressor propagates simultaneously through behaviour, endocrinology, physiology and economic production outcomes rather than through one linear pathway.

nodes.label: Heat Stress in Poultry
nodes.description: The central stressor of the figure: excess environmental thermal load on birds, depicted as solar radiation striking a chicken, which cascades into behavioral, neuroendocrine, physiological and production consequences.
nodes.rationale: Framed as the root cause node because every other category in the figure is drawn downstream of the radiation arrows.

nodes.label: Behavioral Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Spend less time feeding; more time drinking; panting; less moving or walking; wings elevated.
nodes.rationale: These are the only heat-stress responses that are externally visible, which is why they are the tractable target for camera-based automated monitoring rather than blood or hormone assays.

nodes.label: Neuroendocrine Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Increased corticotrophin releasing factor (CRF), adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH), catecholamines and plasma corticosterone; decreased T3, gonadotrophin releasing hormone (GnRH), FSH and LH.
nodes.rationale: Documents the HPA-axis mechanism linking perceived thermal load to suppressed reproduction and growth; requires invasive sampling, so it is background mechanism rather than a monitorable signal.

nodes.label: Physiological Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Oxidative stress; acid-base imbalance; respiratory alkalosis; increase in heterophil/lymphocyte (H/L) ratio; change in cecal microbial profile.
nodes.rationale: Respiratory alkalosis is presented as the direct consequence of panting, tying the behavioral quadrant mechanistically to the physiological quadrant.

nodes.label: Production Changes Under Heat Stress
nodes.description: Increased mortality; decreased feed intake; poor feed conversion ratio; reduced body weight; decreased meat quality; reduced quantity and quality of eggs.
nodes.rationale: Establishes the economic motivation for early heat-stress detection: the losses are realised in production terms, so an early behavioural warning has direct financial value.

edges.source_location: less time feeding -> decreased feed intake
decreased GnRH/FSH/LH -> reduced egg quantity and quality
